newsitem.title: FRANCE: Euro-MPs ratify Energy Charter treaty.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs ratify Energy Charter treaty.

text.p: The European Parliament on Tuesday gave its assent to a pan-European agreement which will set a legally binding framework for trade and investment in energy.
The Energy Charter treaty covers the production, distribution, export and use of energy resources.
It is the first energy cooperation agreement signed by all the former Soviet republics, the countries of central and eastern Europe, the European Union and other industrialised countries.

The United States, although a party to the Energy Charter, has not signed the binding treaty, which focuses on ways of improving security of energy supply, protecting foreign investments and guaranteeing transit arrangements.
The treaty also includes a protocol on energy efficiency and environmental protection.
EU regional affairs commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies told Euro-MPs on Monday the European Commission thought swift ratification of the treaty was of major political and economic importance.
Thirty of the 50 treaty signatories, the number required for the treaty to come into force, are expected to have ratified the treaty by the end of the year.

Nine EU member states have already done so. But Russia, one of the most crucial countries involved, has yet to ratify the accord, which is facing opposition from some members of the Russian Parliament.
Parliament's rapporteur, Swedish Christian Democrat Marjo Matikainen-Kallstrom, on Monday criticised Russia for its failure to ratify the treaty.
She said the East-West accord was vital to prevent trafficking in radioactive substances and improve the safety of Eastern Europe's shaky nuclear reactors.

Matikainen-Kallstrom said there was a crying need to reduce the impact of energy production on the environment and voiced concern that the treaty's provisions on environmental protection were not legally binding.
It was also essential to improve energy efficiency in Central and Eastern Europe, she said, adding that energy savings of 30 to 40 percent were possible.
